newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania Monarchists say vote favours king's return.
newsitem.headline: Albania Monarchists say vote favours king's return.

text.p: Albania's monarchists said on Monday early returns from a referendum held alongside general elections showed voters favoured restoring King Leka to the throne of the impoverished Balkan country.

But with the official count in Sunday's vote barely under way, officials said nothing about the probable outcome. Opposition Socialist leader Fatos Nano has claimed victory in the election over President Sali Berisha's Democrats, saying his party had already won 60 of 115 seats in parliament.
The monarchists said Leka, who returned to Albania last month after nearly 60 years in exile, would win 54 percent of the vote and had scored particularly well in northern regions.
A vote in Leka's favour, they said, would result in immediate restoration of the 1928 royalist constitution.
"Voting in favour of the monarchy would mean bringing back the constitution, the very same day," Fluturak Germenji, spokesman for the monarchist Legality Party, said by telephone.
"All political parties agreed on this in March. Legislation would have to be amended, of course. But the king has the old constitution and no one can alter that, not even parliament."
Officials at the "royal court" in central Tirana, protected by a half dozen burly bodyguards, said Leka would make no public statements pending publication of official results.
Germenji said his party's data showed support for the monarchy hit 75 percent in the northern city of Shkoder, main centre of Albania's Roman Catholic minority.
The capital Tirana had voted 52 percent in favour and even in southern regions, under the control of armed "Citizens Committees", Leka had scored 25 percent, he said.
Berisha agreed to the referendum in March under an accord with 10 parties to form a unity government and hold early elections to end unrest which killed more than 1,500 people.

Leka, who stands 2.04 metres (six foot 10 inches), travelled throughout Albania's backward rural areas but drew only small crowds, especially in Tirana where he concluded his campaign with a message to supporters that he was happy to be among his people and prepared to serve them.
The king has pledged to be a force above politics and restore order within three months of reclaiming his crown.
He is also committed, at least publicly, to restoring "ethnic Albania" -- including Kosovo in former Yugoslavia, where ethnic Albanians outnumber Serbs nine to one, and parts of northern Greece.
Leka fled Albania in 1939 ahead of an invasion by Italian Fascist troops when he was less than a week old. He has since lived in Spain, Britain and most recently in South Africa.
The official ATA news agency quoted court officials as saying Leka saw no difficulty in working with the Socialists.
"I can rule along with the Socialists, like Juan Carlos in Spain," one official, saying he was reflecting Leka's views, was quoted as saying. "But I favour a broad-based government."
Albania has no post-communist constitution, but laws passed since 1990 establish the country as a parliamentary republic.

Nano denounced Berisha as a dictator during the campaign and said it was up to Albanians to choose their form of government, including an "Anglo-Saxon" model if they wished. But he believed voters would reject the monarchy.
"The outcome of the referendum will definitely mean no more chances in Albania for one man one party to run the state system -- be he a president or a king," he said.
Germinji said an outcome favouring Leka would show Albanians returning to their royal roots after 45 years of communism and seven years of political infighting.
"Even the young generation saw him as a symbol of continuity," he said. "Albanians are traditional monarchists, right from the kingdom of Illyria in Roman times."
